rationale: Both warn of a coming period of religious danger. First Timothy says the Spirit speaks about later times and departure from faith; Second Timothy says last days and difficult times. The time expressions and particular warnings are not identified as a dated timetable.

Both lists include arrogance, boasting and disobedience to parents, alongside greed or love of money. Romans gives its wider account of wrongdoing; Timothy's letter introduces conduct in difficult times. Neither list is silently made identical to the other.

Both vice catalogues name slander and the lack of natural affection. Each includes other faults and its own context. Timothy's irreconcilability, savagery and lack of self-control are not supplied as additional words in Romans.

Loving pleasure rather than God corresponds to John's contrast between loving the world and the Father's love. John specifies worldly desires and their passing; Timothy's list also names betrayal, recklessness and conceit. Pleasure and world are not treated as identical printed categories.

Both expose a gap between outward religious profession and denial. Titus says people profess knowing God but deny Him by works; Timothy's letter names a form of godliness with denial of its power. The different objects of denial are preserved.

Both describe deceptive people gaining control through desires. Peter names enticement and slavery to corruption; Timothy's letter names entering houses and taking captive particular weak women burdened with sins. It neither extends that description to all women nor supplies an unprinted sexual act.

Always learning without arriving at knowledge of truth contrasts with the hope that God may grant repentance toward knowledge of truth. The source's captive-learning context and the opponents addressed in the correction instruction are not declared the same people.

Exodus records Pharaoh's experts countering Moses and Aaron through rival staff signs. This provides a Moses-opposition comparison for the letter's Jannes-and-Jambres analogy. Exodus does not name those two men or independently establish each man's identity.

The enchanters cannot produce the gnats and acknowledge God's finger, giving a specific episode where opposing expertise meets a visible limit. Timothy's letter compares the exposure of its opponents' folly to those earlier men. Exodus does not supply the names Jannes and Jambres.

Corinthians asks readers to imitate Paul and says Timothy will remind them of his ways and teaching in Christ. Timothy's letter says he followed Paul's teaching and conduct with named virtues. Their teaching/example relation does not identify every virtue or circumstance as the same episode.

Acts narrates Paul's stoning, his rising, and the ministry route through Lystra, Iconium and Antioch. The letter recalls persecutions in those named places and the Lord's rescue. This connects the specific locations and suffering without calculating an unprinted date or making every incident identical.

Jesus says that if people persecuted Him they will persecute His servants; Timothy's letter says those seeking godly life in Christ will be persecuted. The slave/master explanation and the godly-life formulation remain distinct.

Advancing ungodliness and spreading false teaching in the earlier warning form a specific internal counterpart to evil impostors going from bad to worse. The named resurrection-error teachers are not asserted to be every person covered by this later general warning.

Both tell Timothy to retain instruction received from known teachers. The earlier command explicitly names words heard from Paul in faith and love; this one refers plurally to those from whom he learned. The plural is not reduced to Paul alone.

Jesus connects the Scriptures' testimony to Him with coming to Him for life. Timothy's letter names sacred writings known from infancy that make wise for salvation through faith in Christ. Neither passage says bare literacy alone saves or defines the whole later canon's extent.

Both connect scriptural witness with God rather than merely human initiative. Peter speaks of prophecy and people carried by the Holy Spirit; Timothy's letter says all Scripture is God-breathed and names its uses. Prophecy and all Scripture are not silently made identical scopes.

Both name equipping people for good action. Hebrews prays for God to equip the readers to do His will; Timothy's letter gives Scripture's outcome as the person of God being equipped for every good work. Their agents and immediate explanations remain distinct.

Both explicitly name Christ's judgment of the living and dead. Acts places it in the commanded proclamation about God's appointed judge; Timothy's letter gives a charge before God and Christ and names His appearing and kingdom. The speech settings differ.

Both commission speaking, exhortation and rebuke. Titus names authority and not being disregarded; Timothy's letter names proclaiming the word, readiness in and out of season, patience and teaching. Each charge keeps its specific terms.

Both portray hearers resisting truthful instruction and seeking a message suited to their own wishes. Isaiah records demands made to prophetic speakers; Timothy's letter describes accumulating teachers according to desires. The addressed people and historical setting are not made identical.

Both contrast truth with myths and turning away. Titus names Jewish myths and commands of people who turn from truth; Timothy's letter names hearing turning from truth toward myths. The particular qualifiers in Titus are not imposed on every hearer here.

The command to fulfill service corresponds to the instruction that Archippus attend to and fulfill the service received in the Lord. Timothy is also told to be sober, endure and do an evangelist's work; Colossians does not assign that same title to Archippus.

Both use being poured out in a ministry and offering context. Philippians states the image conditionally and relates it to the readers' faith; Timothy's letter says already and names departure's time. No death method or date is supplied by this comparison.

Paul in Acts speaks of finishing his course and service received from the Lord Jesus; the letter says the course has been finished and the faith kept. The intended goal and completed-course statement are preserved without fixing a chronology from the comparison alone.

Both connect a crown promised by the Lord with enduring fidelity and love. James names the crown of life after testing; Timothy's letter names righteousness's crown, the righteous Judge and love of His appearing. The distinct crown titles and conditions remain as printed.

The later command repeats the effort to come and specifies before winter, supplying a concrete counterpart to come to me soon. It concerns the same letter's addressed visitor without explaining every name in the following greetings.

Philemon names Demas among Paul's fellow workers. Timothy's letter reports his desertion and love for the present age and names Thessalonica. The descriptions differ; the comparison does not date the letters or fill in Crescens's and Titus's journeys.

relationship: named Mark and Luke service context
rationale: Both explicitly name Luke and Mark among Paul's associates. Philemon calls its group fellow workers; Timothy's letter names Luke's presence and asks for Mark as useful for service. The personal circumstances and tasks remain distinct.

Both name Tychicus in a sending and ministry context. Ephesians describes his report and encouragement mission; Timothy's letter states sending him to Ephesus. No identical delivery date or additional itinerary is established.

relationship: visit request and items to bring
rationale: The earlier request that Timothy come soon supplies the concrete visit context for when you come and the cloak, books and parchments request. The link does not infer an illness, a cause for needing the cloak or the contents of the books.

The Lord's repayment of Alexander according to his works corresponds to the statement that God repays each according to works. The named coppersmith is not identified as another Alexander from a name alone, nor is a precise penalty supplied.

Alexander the coppersmith in the preceding notice supplies the referent of him against whom Timothy must guard himself. The instruction adds his opposition to their words, without identifying him with every other named Alexander.

Both ask that wrongdoing not be counted against the people responsible. Stephen prays over his attackers while dying; Paul speaks of those who deserted him at his first defense. The actions and legal circumstances are not treated as identical.

Acts says the Lord stood by Paul and connected courage with testimony in Jerusalem and Rome. Timothy's letter says the Lord stood beside and strengthened him for proclamation to the nations. The similar support and witness language does not identify the two occasions.

The Psalm's request for rescue from a lion's mouth corresponds to Paul's statement of being rescued from a lion's mouth. The prayer and reported rescue differ; the phrase does not establish that Paul faced a literal lion or identify the two speakers' circumstances.

The prayer to be delivered from the evil one relates to confidence that the Lord will rescue Paul from every evil work and save him into the heavenly kingdom. The communal prayer and personal assurance have different objects and do not equate every evil work with one named agent.

Both greet the named Prisca and Aquila. Romans also names their work, risk and the Church in their house; Timothy's letter separately greets Onesiphorus's household. The two households are not merged.

Both name Trophimus in association with Paul. Acts explicitly calls him the Ephesian and describes seeing him with Paul; Timothy's letter names leaving him sick in Miletus. It does not date the sickness or make it the cause of the temple accusation, and supplies no new Erastus identity.

Make every effort to come before winter develops the earlier request to make every effort to come soon. This identifies the same letter's practical travel request, without supplying biographies or tasks for the uniquely named greeters in the rest of the unit.

Both close with the Lord, grace and the recipients' spirit in view. Galatians explicitly names our Lord Jesus Christ, brothers and Amen; Timothy's letter has the separate Lord-with-your-spirit and grace-with-you-all statements. Its shorter actual wording is not expanded.
